newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: CBOT wheat extends rally in Asia on supply fears.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat extends rally in Asia on supply fears.

text.p: World wheat prices surged to new highs in Asian trade on Tuesday extending overnight gains in Chicago, where futures hit a seven-month peak, on fears for the U.S. spring crop after unseasonal freezing temperatures.
Indications of emerging drought in wheat growing areas in France and Australia gave a further upward twist to prices amid growing concerns over a squeeze on world grain supplies.

Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures rose 12 cents a bushel to $4.35 a bushel on the exchange's Project A after hours trading system, before pulling back to $4.29-3/4 by 0700 GMT. "We're watching and waiting for further developments in wheat," said a trader with South Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF).
"But we expect some kind of short term correction in corn and soybean prices as the nearby contracts don't appear to be affected by wheat any more and have been falling slightly."
CBOT May soybeans were down 1-1/2 cents at $8.31-1/2 a bushel on Project A after closing the open outcry session 2-1/2 cents firmer in Chicago on Monday at $8.33.
May corn was down one cent at $3.02-3/4 a bushel.
Australian wheat futures also forged ahead on Tuesday in line with Chicago.
Settlement prices rose across the board in Sydney with near-term contracts up by about $A4.50 a tonne, November 1997 up $9.00 and more distant contracts up by $7.00.

The jump in world wheat prices may make major buyer Japan postpone some of its wheat buying, but drastic cuts in imports are unlikely due to the country's tradition of constant grain purchasing, the Food Agency and traders said on Tuesday.
"We'd like to confirm actual losses in U.S. wheat export capacity as soon as possible," said Shinichi Yahagi, director of the Food Agency's trade division.
The Food Agency is the sole importer of wheat, barley and rice in Japan, and has an import tender every Thursday.
"If buying prices exceed our target prices, we may need to consider postponing some of our wheat imports by weeks. But at this stage, we have no such plan," Yahagi said.
Local trade houses said the Food Agency will maintain its regular wheat imports despite the Chicago rally.
"Even when the wheat market hit a record high last year, they remained a constant buyer. Their buying pattern is different from others in Southeast Asia," one trader said.
He said the Food Agency can shift to cheaper wheat, if U.S. origin stays above its target buying prices.
One Food Agency source noted that the agency is under increasing pressure to buy lower-priced grain.
